policy: A decision must name what was examined and carry conditions re-evaluated on every run. Having a control is not evidence that a requirement is met: no PASS may be inferred from the presence of MFA, RLS, CodeQL, an SBOM or a passing test. Anything without a valid, currently-holding decision stays PENDING and NOT_ASSESSED.

conditions.condition: validation is implemented in code, so a document has something to describe
the security documentation set still defines no input validation rules

decisions.note: Validation is implemented but undocumented. Neither the threat model nor the security policy defines how data items are checked against an expected structure, so there is no stated rule an implementation could be measured against. This condition watches those two documents; a rules document added elsewhere would need this decision revisited.

conditions.condition: the platform combines related data items whose consistency would have to be defined
no document defines the logical or contextual consistency expected of combined data items

decisions.note: The code enforces real cross-entity consistency, but no document states what consistency is expected. An undocumented rule cannot be reviewed, and a reviewer cannot tell an intended rule from an accidental one.

conditions.condition: no document states business logic limits, per-user or global

decisions.note: No documented expectation exists for business logic limits, either per user or across the application. This is the gap that also makes V2.3.2 unverifiable.

evidence: dto-scan:every DTO file in the API declares field constraints

conditions.condition: the global validation pipe is installed at the service entry point
the pipe rejects values that do not satisfy the declared constraints

decisions.note: Input is checked against per-field constraints declared on the DTOs rather than accepted and inspected later. Every DTO file in apps/api/src carries class-validator constraints, and the global pipe applies them before a handler runs.

conditions.condition: validation runs in the trusted service layer

decisions.note: Validation is enforced server-side by a global pipe, not by the client. Stated plainly: whitelist strips undeclared properties rather than rejecting the request, because forbidNonWhitelisted is false. That satisfies enforcement at a trusted layer, and it is the one place the control is weaker than it could be.

conditions.condition: cross-entity consistency is enforced on at least the lab finalisation command

decisions.note: Applicability decided; assessment deliberately not claimed. On the lab finalisation command the check is exemplary: the sample must belong to the deal and the tenant, its chain of custody must be complete, the signed evidence must be purpose-bound to that sample, shipment, acceptance, lab and protocol number, and the actor must hold signatory authority at that moment. The other commands in the policy table have not been examined, so the requirement is not claimed as met for the application.

conditions.condition: every command declares the status it may be issued from and the roles that may issue it
the authoritative path rejects a command issued from any other status

decisions.note: Deal actions are declared with an explicit from/to pair, and the PostgreSQL authority path rejects any command whose stored status does not match definition.from - inside the transaction that already holds the advisory lock, so the check cannot be raced. This decision covers that authoritative path. A second, different transition map exists in runtime-core/runtime-state-machine.ts, used only by runtime-core.service.ts; it is not what this PASS rests on.

conditions.condition: there is still no documented limit for an implementation to be measured against

decisions.note: The requirement asks that limits be implemented per the documentation. No documentation of business logic limits exists, so no implementation can be verified against it. This fails on the same gap as V2.1.3 and is recorded separately because closing V2.1.3 alone would not close this one.

conditions.condition: deal commands execute inside the shared transactional context
that context is a database transaction with an explicit isolation level

decisions.note: A deal command runs entirely inside one database transaction opened by RlsTransactionService, so it either completes or leaves no partial state. Isolation is explicit rather than implicit, and serializable transactions carry a bounded retry.

conditions.condition: a per-deal lock is taken before any state is read
the contended rows are read under a row lock

decisions.note: Concurrent commands against one deal serialise on a transaction-scoped advisory lock keyed by the deal id, taken as the first statement in the transaction, and the contended rows are read FOR UPDATE. Two requests cannot both act on the same pre-state.

conditions.condition: high-value money movement exists as a single command
no second-approver requirement guards it
a second-approval control does exist elsewhere, on the authority-granting path

decisions.note: Release of funds is issued by one actor holding one role: the command policy carries BANK_RELEASE_REQUEST with no second-approver requirement, so the high-value money flow this requirement targets is unprotected. Correction to the note this decision first carried: it claimed no dual-approval control existed anywhere in the tree. That was false. accounting-authority-command.policy.ts implements a real one for granting signing authority - self-approval is forbidden, the second approver must be a different person from both the actor and the target, and that person must hold SIGNING_AUTHORITY_MANAGE with MFA verified within 300 seconds. The gap is that this control guards who may hold authority, not who may move money. The earlier note also equated this gap with the standing four-eyes governance blocker; that blocker concerns independent code review and is a different control.

conditions.condition: the export controller serves bulk data
it still carries no anti-automation control

decisions.note: Rate limiting exists on authentication and a few deal endpoints, but the endpoints that return bulk data carry none - and those are the ones the requirement names, because they are the exfiltration surface. nginx declares limit_req zones, but that configuration is referenced by no deployment file in the repository, so it cannot be shown to apply.

conditions.condition: rapid-submission detection exists
the authoritative command path does not consult it

decisions.note: Rapid-transition detection exists and scores, but it prevents nothing: it is reachable only through its own controller endpoint, the deal command path never calls it, and a flagged score is logged and persisted rather than refused. Its state is also an in-process Map, so it would not survive more than one instance.

conditions.condition: the upload route still carries no reference to a documented upload policy
the upload route is the surface the missing documentation would have to cover

decisions.note: No document defines the permitted file types, expected extensions or maximum size for this upload feature. Unpacked size is the sharpest gap: it is stated nowhere, and decompression itself is uncapped (see V5.2.3). Stated precisely, because the first version of this note said unpacked size was "neither stated nor bounded anywhere" and that was too broad: extracted text is truncated at MAX_EXTRACTED_CHARS and OCR output is bounded by the execFile maxBuffer. Those bound what is kept, not what is inflated, so the requirement still fails - but the note should not suggest that nothing limits anything.

conditions.condition: the size caps exist and are applied in the handler
no ceiling is applied before the body is buffered

decisions.note: The caps (4 files, 8 MiB per file, 24 MiB total) are enforced only after request.formData() has buffered the entire body. The single pre-buffer check trusts a client-supplied Content-Length and is skipped when that header is absent, so an oversized body is read into memory before it is rejected. nginx sets client_max_body_size 10m, but that is an infrastructure ceiling whose deployment cannot be verified from the repository.

conditions.condition: dispatch is driven by the filename extension
no content-based file type detection is performed

decisions.note: Processing is selected purely from the filename extension. Nothing inspects the file signature, and the reported mediaType is echoed from the client-controlled file.type. A file may declare any extension its content does not match.

conditions.condition: the route decompresses archive and stream content
no ceiling is placed on decompressed output

decisions.note: inflateRawSync (docx member) and inflateSync (PDF FlateDecode streams) are called without maxOutputLength, and no cap on the number of archive entries exists. A compression bomb inside word/document.xml or a PDF stream inflates without a ceiling inside the request handler.

conditions.condition: only per-request caps exist
no per-user quota or stored-file accounting exists

decisions.note: The route enforces per-request limits only. There is no per-user file-count or storage quota, and no accounting that would let one be enforced.

conditions.condition: archive members are read into memory by exact name, never written out
no archive extraction to disk exists that a symlink member could target

decisions.note: No archive member is ever written to the filesystem. zipEntry locates one member by exact name and returns its bytes, so an archive cannot introduce a symlink.

conditions.condition: uploaded images are passed to an image pipeline
no pixel-dimension limit is applied

decisions.note: Uploaded images go straight to normalisation and OCR with no maximum pixel dimension. The 30 s OCR timeout limits the damage but is not the control this requirement asks for.

conditions.condition: working files are written only to a private temporary directory
no uploaded content is written into a web-served directory

decisions.note: Uploaded content is never stored in a public folder. Working files live in a per-request mkdtemp directory under the OS temp path, are written with mode 0600 and removed afterwards, so nothing uploaded is reachable as a server-side program or a static asset.

conditions.condition: every on-disk path is internally generated
the submitted filename is never used to build a path

decisions.note: File paths are built from internally generated names inside a random temporary directory. The submitted filename is retained only as a truncated display label and is never used to construct a path.

conditions.condition: decompression targets one member matched by exact name
no archive-supplied path is joined onto a filesystem path

decisions.note: Path information carried inside an archive is never used. The single member is matched by an exact literal name and its bytes are kept in memory, so zip slip has no route to the filesystem.

conditions.condition: a user-supplied route parameter is still interpolated into a download filename
the parameter is still unvalidated at the controller

decisions.note: exportLedger interpolates the raw @Param('dealId') into the Content-Disposition filename. The parameter is a bare string, so neither ParseUUIDPipe nor the global ValidationPipe constrains it, and the application neither validates nor ignores the user-submitted component.

conditions.condition: download filenames are still emitted as a bare quoted string
no RFC 6266 encoding is applied

decisions.note: Content-Disposition is built as a bare quoted string with no RFC 6266 encoding and no sanitisation of the interpolated value. A quote in dealId breaks the quoted-string. Node refuses CR and LF in header values, so header injection is blocked by the platform rather than by the application.

conditions.condition: the route accepts files from untrusted sources
no antivirus integration exists anywhere in application or package source

decisions.note: Files accepted from untrusted sources are parsed and their text returned with no malware scanning. docs/security/THREAT_MODEL.md already names malware scan and quarantine as a required control; it is not implemented.

conditions.condition: the API verifier checks the signature before reading any claim
the web verifier returns the payload only after the MAC verifies

decisions.note: Both token verifiers in the tree check the signature or MAC before any claim is read. The web verifier decodes the payload only after crypto.subtle.verify returns true; the API verifier reads claims only from the value jwt.verify returned.

conditions.condition: the API verifier still states no algorithm allowlist
the web verifier does state one

decisions.note: The two verifiers disagree. The web verifier rejects any header whose alg is not HS256 before verifying - that is the allowlist the requirement asks for. The API verifier passes no algorithms option to jwt.verify. jsonwebtoken 9 refuses alg none and, given a string secret, restricts itself to HMAC, so the protection is real - but it comes from a library default rather than from a stated allowlist, and a future dependency change or a switch to a key object would move it silently. The requirement asks for the allowlist to be stated.

conditions.condition: the API key material comes from a required pre-configured secret
no verifier resolves key material from a token-supplied source

decisions.note: Validation keys come from configuration, not from the token. There is no JWKS endpoint, no remote key set and no kid-directed key lookup anywhere, so a token cannot nominate the key that verifies it.

conditions.condition: the API issues a bounded lifetime and verifies it
the web verifier rejects an expired or not-yet-valid token

decisions.note: Access tokens carry a 15 minute expiry that jwt.verify enforces, and the web verifier checks both exp and nbf against the supplied time. A token outside its validity span is refused by both paths.

conditions.condition: the API verifier does check the token type
the web verifier still checks neither type nor audience
the cabinet session route signs and verifies with the API token secret

decisions.note: The API verifier does this correctly: it rejects a token whose typ is not access. The web verifier does not check type at all, and the cabinet session route hands it process.env.JWT_SECRET - the same secret the API signs access tokens with. So any HS256 token signed with that secret verifies there regardless of what it was issued for. In practice an access token yields no cabinet role because it carries no role claim, but that is a behavioural accident, not a type check. The staff route is not part of this gap: it does check purpose-bearing claims (owner, testAccess, sub, email) after verifying.

conditions.condition: the API verifier does constrain the audience
the web verifier still applies no audience restriction

decisions.note: The API verifier passes an audience to jwt.verify, so a token minted for another audience is refused there. The web verifier applies no audience restriction, so it accepts tokens not intended for it. One of the two services meets the requirement; the requirement is about the service receiving the token, and one of them does not.

conditions.condition: issued access tokens carry an audience restriction

decisions.note: One private key is used to issue tokens for more than one consumer - the API access token and the web cabinet session token share JWT_SECRET - which is exactly the situation this requirement addresses. Issued access tokens do carry an audience restriction, so the token itself states who it is for. Whether every receiver enforces that restriction is a separate matter, and it is recorded as failing under V9.2.3.

conditions.condition: the production edge is still Caddy on a single REG.RU virtual server
that host is still the sole production host

decisions.note: Applicability decided; assessment blocked on evidence this programme cannot gather. The production TLS terminator is Caddy on the REG.RU virtual server, and its configuration is not in the repository - the runbook treats Compose, Caddy and environment as protected artifacts held on the host. infra/nginx/nginx.conf is NOT the production terminator and is not evidence about production. Verifying this requirement needs a scan of the live endpoint or the edge configuration itself. Asserting a PASS from what Caddy does by default would be an inference, not evidence. Specifically unverified here: which TLS protocol versions are enabled.

conditions.condition: no application code reads or validates a client certificate identity

decisions.note: The requirement governs an application that uses an mTLS client certificate identity for authentication or authorisation. No application code reads or validates such an identity anywhere. Integration adapters mention mTLS in prose as a vendor transport concern, but prose is not a code path. If a certificate identity is ever consumed, this condition stops holding and the requirement returns to assessment.

conditions.condition: the telemetry exporter still defaults to a plaintext endpoint
the endpoint validator still accepts a plaintext scheme

decisions.note: The requirement names monitoring explicitly. The telemetry exporter defaults to a plaintext endpoint and its validator accepts http: on purpose, so traces leave the process unencrypted unless an operator overrides the variable. infra/istio/peer-authentication.yml declares STRICT mesh mTLS, but it does not rescue this: production is a single REG.RU virtual server running Docker Compose, not a Kubernetes cluster, and the platform own UI copy states the mesh is a target model pending a live cluster. Nothing wraps this traffic.

conditions.condition: certificate verification is explicit where a TLS socket is opened directly
nothing in the tree disables certificate verification

decisions.note: Where the application opens a TLS socket itself it sets rejectUnauthorized: true rather than relying on a default. Everywhere else it uses fetch, which verifies by default, and nothing anywhere turns verification off: the tree contains no rejectUnauthorized: false and no NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED. The control is both asserted and not undone.

conditions.condition: the search client still targets a plaintext endpoint
the model client still targets a plaintext endpoint
the web tier still reaches the API over a plaintext base

decisions.note: Internal HTTP traffic between services is plaintext by default on every hop examined: web to API, API to Elasticsearch, API to the model service. No configuration path requires a TLS scheme for any of them. As with V12.3.1, the Istio STRICT mTLS policy does not apply - production is Docker Compose on one virtual server, not a mesh.

conditions.condition: internal hops still carry no TLS for a certificate to be trusted on

decisions.note: This requirement governs which certificates internal TLS connections trust. There are no internal TLS connections to hold certificates, so the requirement is unmet rather than inapplicable: the prerequisite is missing. Recorded separately from V12.3.3 because closing V12.3.3 would not automatically satisfy it - the certificates introduced would then have to be trusted ones.

conditions.condition: one internal hop is authenticated by a signed request
the model-service hop still sends no credential of any kind
the search hop authenticates with a shared password rather than a signature

decisions.note: The three internal hops authenticate in three different ways, and only one is sound. Web to API signs each request with HMAC-SHA256 over a version, method, canonical path, timestamp and body hash, deriving the URL from the signed path constant so a signature can never cover a path other than the one dialled. API to Elasticsearch sends HTTP basic auth when ELASTICSEARCH_PASSWORD is set - a shared secret, and by V12.3.3 it travels over plaintext http, so the credential itself is exposed on the wire. API to the model service sends only Content-Type and no credential at all. Correction to the note this decision first carried: it said the other hops had no service token, signature or shared secret. That was wrong about Elasticsearch, and the condition that was meant to catch it searched for the wrong words - it looked for "authorization" where the file says "auth:" and "password". Both are fixed here.

conditions.condition: no WebRTC API is referenced anywhere in application or package source
no WebRTC dependency is declared in any tracked manifest

decisions.note: The platform exposes no real-time peer connection, media capture or data channel surface. This chapter is out of scope while that remains true; the conditions are re-evaluated on every run, so introducing WebRTC restores the requirements to assessment.
